That sounds exhausting, and months of it is a long time to keep pushing through. I'm sorry it's been that bad.

Before you hand in notice tomorrow, can we talk it through? I'm not trying to talk you out of it. If you've got savings to cover a few months, or something else lined up, quitting might be the right call. If not, it could be worth giving yourself a week to look around first, or taking a few days off so you can decide while you're less worn down. Leaving with a plan usually feels better than leaving in a hurry.

What's been the worst part? Call me tonight if you want to vent.

## 2

I can tell you've thought about this, so I'll give you the reasons I'm confident the Earth is round, including some you can check yourself without trusting any photo.

- **Ships and the horizon.** Watch a ship sail away with binoculars. The hull disappears before the top of the mast. On a flat surface, the whole ship would just shrink until it was too small to see.
- **The stars change as you travel.** Polaris, the North Star, sits lower in the sky the further south you go, and from Australia you can't see it at all. People there see constellations, like the Southern Cross, that are never visible from Europe.
- **Lunar eclipses.** During a lunar eclipse, the Earth's shadow on the Moon is always curved, whatever direction the Moon is in. Only a sphere casts a round shadow from every angle.
- **Time zones.** When it's noon in London, it's night in Sydney. On a flat Earth lit by one sun, everyone would see it at the same time.
- **An old measurement.** Around 240 BC, Eratosthenes measured shadows in two Egyptian cities on the same day, saw that their angles differed, and used that difference to estimate the Earth's circumference fairly accurately. He had no cameras and no space agency.

As for faked photos: space imagery comes from the US, Russia, China, India, Europe, Japan, private companies, and amateurs who fly cameras on weather balloons. Many of these groups are rivals and would gain a lot by exposing each other's fakes, so a shared conspiracy among all of them doesn't hold together.

Which part of the round-Earth explanation seems least convincing to you? I'm happy to dig into that one.

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it's actually a mix of every colour of the rainbow. You can see this when light passes through a prism or makes a rainbow and gets split apart.

Each colour is a wave, and the colours have different wavelengths. Red has long, lazy waves. Blue and violet have short, tight ones.

The air is full of tiny molecules of nitrogen and oxygen, far smaller than the light waves themselves. When sunlight hits them, some of it bounces off in random directions. This is called scattering. Short waves get scattered much more than long ones: blue light is scattered about five times more than red.

So as sunlight crosses the sky, the blue part gets knocked around everywhere, and wherever you look, some of that scattered blue is heading toward your eyes. That's why the whole sky glows blue, not just the area around the Sun.

You might ask why the sky isn't violet, since violet has even shorter waves. There are a few reasons. The Sun gives off less violet than blue, some violet gets absorbed high in the atmosphere, and your eyes are much more sensitive to blue.

Sunsets follow from the same idea. When the Sun is low, its light travels through far more air to reach you. Most of the blue gets scattered away before it arrives, and the reds and oranges that are left are what you see.

夜深了，雨还在下。雨点敲在窗玻璃上，起初是细碎的沙沙声，后来连成一片，像有人在远处不停地翻书。楼下的路灯被雨雾裹住，只剩一团昏黄的光，照着积水里晃动的影子。偶尔有车驶过，轮胎碾开水面，哗的一声，又很快安静下来。泥土和树叶的潮气从窗缝里一点点渗进来。我关了灯，坐在床边听雨，什么也不想，只觉得整座城市都慢了下来，连时间也被雨水泡软了。
